title: Rethinking One Gene, One Token: Transcriptome-Aware Tokenization for Single-Cell Foundation Models
summary: scTAT replaces one-token-per-gene with a gene-set vocabulary of overlapping sets that recur with stable relative expression across the pretraining corpus, plus a per-cell tokenizer that lets gene sets and single genes compete for token positions (scores normalised by √set size). Training still reconstructs individual genes, so outputs stay at gene resolution.
takeaways: Which genes share a token is decided per cell, not fixed in advance.
Matches the strongest one-gene-per-token model on frozen-embedding cell-type annotation with half the token budget; the advantage grows as the budget shrinks.
Gene-set tokens nearly halve the Transformer's matmul cost for the same genes.
relevance: Grouping co-expressed features into shared tokens while decoding at fine resolution is close to the gene → isoform hierarchy in scIso: a gene token that is decoded into its isoform composition is the same pattern one level down. Pairs well with your Set Transformer note on treating expression as a set.

title: Masked diffusion as random sequential adsorption: an exactly solvable model for parallel decoding
summary: Shows that the error of revealing several tokens in parallel in a masked diffusion model equals the entropy production of generation relative to the reversed masking process. For Markov data the generation is a random sequential adsorption process that is solved exactly for any number of steps, and for many steps the error becomes a dissipation set by a closed-form thermodynamic metric built from mutual information between tokens.
takeaways: Parallel-decoding error = entropy production relative to the reversed masking process, for any data.
Optimal unmasking schedules are geodesics of a thermodynamic metric derived from inter-token mutual information.
With longer-range correlations the error concentrates early, so schedules that start with small steps do better and need fewer steps.
relevance: Directly informs schedule design for your masked-diffusion model of isoform counts: isoforms within a gene are strongly correlated, which this analysis says should push you toward small early unmasking steps. It is also a neat bridge between your DISC and GEO tracks (schedules as geodesics).

title: A Night at the LLM Zoo: Data Conditioned Flow Matching for Generating Pretrained LLM Weights
summary: The authors train a zoo of GPT-2 models (51M, 124M and 355M parameters, 100 per size) while systematically varying the pretraining data mixture, then fit a flow-matching model of full weights in a Gram-PCA compressed weight space, conditioned on the mixture composition. Generated models for held-out mixtures perform similarly to trained ones on perplexity and capability benchmarks.
takeaways: Variation across the zoo is structured by data-mixture composition.
Conditioning on a point on the simplex of mixtures lets the generator generalise zero-shot to unseen mixtures.
Weight generation is made tractable by compressing weights (Gram-PCA) before flow matching.
relevance: An exploratory spark: flow matching conditioned on a composition (a point on the simplex) is the mirror image of your setting, where the composition is the output. A fun example to show students in the course of how far 'generate X with flow matching' now reaches.

title: Coupling cellular trajectories and RNA kinetics on continuous expression manifolds with ManifoldVelo
authors: Zhou, Li, Liu, Pan et al.
summary: ManifoldVelo jointly learns cell coordinates (pseudotime), continuous unspliced/spliced RNA trajectories and regulatory kinetics, matching trajectory derivatives to transcription–splicing–degradation dynamics, also between observed cells. It handles cyclic, multibranch and smooth trajectories, and new cells get pseudotime and velocity from spliced RNA alone without refitting.
takeaways: Pseudotime and RNA velocity are estimated together, so ordering, reconstruction and kinetics inform each other instead of being fitted in sequence.
Kinetic consistency is enforced on a continuous manifold, including between observed cells, rather than only at data points.
The fitted model works as a reusable dynamic reference: new samples are projected using spliced counts only.
relevance: Splicing kinetics enter here through unspliced/spliced counts per gene; it is a useful contrast to your isoform-level view, where splicing shows up as compositions over isoforms with a fixed gene total — and a reminder that time/trajectory could be a conditioning variable for scIso-style prediction.

title: Logical Guidance of Stochastic Interpolants
authors: Gerhartz, Alesiani, Warrell, Christiansen et al.
summary: The paper asks when logical combinations of conditions (negation, XOR, conjunction) can be imposed by composing velocity fields in flow matching / stochastic interpolants. Negation and exclusive disjunction compose exactly on any interpolant, but conjunction is exact only on Gaussian paths; LOGSI fixes this by alternating transport steps with score-based re-equilibration.
takeaways: Score composition rules from diffusion do not carry over to velocities for free: conjunction incurs a drift-interaction error on non-Gaussian paths.
Negation and XOR remain exact for any interpolant, so some guidance logic is path-independent.
LOGSI interleaves transport with score re-equilibration and improves rule conformity at equal compute on images and QM9 molecular editing.
relevance: If you want to guide your lattice-simplex / generator-matching models on several conditions at once (cell type AND perturbation, say), this paper shows exactly where naive composition of learned fields stops being exact — worth knowing before trying it on non-Gaussian paths.

title: Learning hidden-state dynamics from unpaired snapshots with lift-project SDEs
summary: From unpaired population snapshots, methods that evolve only the observed coordinate (time-dependent SDEs, Schrödinger bridges, OT) are shown, for a scalar observation, to always have non-negative lagged covariance — a computable error floor. The lift-project SDE adds a few hidden coordinates, trained only to match the snapshots, and gets below that floor on oscillator benchmarks.
takeaways: Snapshot data fixes marginals but not temporal coupling; the modelling prior decides the coupling.
Observed-only Markov models cannot produce negative lagged covariance (via a comparison theorem), so oscillatory dynamics are out of reach.
One hidden coordinate already helps, and one model can fit experiments that differ only in hidden initial state.
relevance: A spark from dynamical systems: single-cell snapshot methods (Schrödinger bridges, OT trajectory inference) are exactly the observed-only class critiqued here, which makes it a thought-provoking angle on latent states in cell dynamics.

title: IsoAlign: Isoform-Aware DNA-Protein Alignment via Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
summary: Genomic foundation models usually ignore alternative splicing. IsoAlign pretrains DNA representations by aligning transcripts to their protein isoforms with two JEPA objectives: DP-JEPA predicts protein embeddings from DNA with contrastive alignment, and IM-JEPA masks protein isoforms of the same gene and predicts them from the others.
takeaways: Isoform-level DNA-protein pairing is used as the pretraining signal, rather than plain masked-token prediction on DNA.
IM-JEPA explicitly models relationships among the alternative isoforms of one gene via masked prediction in protein-embedding space.
The authors report improved downstream performance on pathogenicity, fitness, gene-expression and TF-binding tasks over standard self-supervised GFM pretraining.
relevance: IM-JEPA's 'predict a masked isoform from its siblings within a gene' is the sequence-side analogue of your within-gene compositional view of isoform counts; its isoform embeddings could be a useful per-isoform feature for scIso or for conditioning a lattice-simplex generator.

title: Coarse-Graining Optimal Transport for Rollout-Free Post-Training of Flow Matching
summary: Making flow-matching couplings more OT-like does not reliably help at low NFE, because the source is continuous, targets are finite and networks have finite capacity. ReCouple builds controllable coarse-grained OT couplings for rollout-free post-training; ReCouple+ refines source resolution toward semi-discrete OT, and ReCouple++ adds spatial regularisation of the velocity field.
takeaways: Coupling optimality, neural realizability and sample quality interact in an NFE-dependent way — 'more OT' is not automatically better.
Coarse-graining the OT coupling gives a knob between independent and fully OT couplings, used to post-train an existing flow without simulating rollouts.
Straight trajectories need not mean spatially simple velocity fields, which motivates regularising the velocity field itself (ReCouple++).
relevance: Directly relevant to your OT-CFM / minibatch-OT background and to choosing couplings for simplex flow matching: the finding that coupling optimality must be traded against what the network can represent is a useful lens for isoform-proportion flows with few sampling steps.

title: Steerable Single-step Retrosynthesis with Electron-pushing Discrete Flow Matching and Feynman-Kac Steering
summary: Verso MAELLE represents a retrosynthetic disconnection as a CTMC over edits in 'electron space' (electron-pushing arrows) and trains it with discrete flow matching. At inference, Feynman-Kac steering with rewards pushes it toward under-represented reaction types, e.g. ring-forming cyclisations and domino sequences.
takeaways: The CTMC state space is chosen to match domain mechanics (electron redistribution) rather than generic tokens or graph edits.
Feynman-Kac (SMC-style) steering lets a pretrained discrete flow be redirected by a reward without retraining.
Steering can reach modes the training data under-represents, shown with a ring-breaking reward and a domino-incentivising reward.
relevance: A spark from chemistry, but methodologically close to home: a CTMC on a domain-shaped discrete state space plus reward-based FK steering mirrors your lattice-simplex generator matching, and suggests how one could steer isoform-count samples toward e.g. a desired isoform switch.

title: CytoWave: Perturbation-Centric Pretraining for Single-Cell Response Prediction
summary: CytoWave is a pretraining framework for predicting single-cell responses to genetic perturbations. It unifies large cross-species perturbation datasets via orthology, first learns control cell states with masked gene-expression recovery, then pretrains to predict perturbed expression from control state plus perturbation signal, with a contrastive term aligning response latents to perturbation embeddings.
takeaways: Two-stage training: masked recovery on unperturbed cells, then perturbation-conditioned prediction.
Orthology mapping lets perturbation screens from several species be pooled for pretraining.
Evaluation holds out whole datasets, a stricter test of generalisation than within-dataset splits.
relevance: A useful reference point for perturbation modelling as conditional prediction from a control state — the same "predict expression given context" framing as scIso, and a reminder to evaluate with dataset-level hold-outs.

title: Online Class Posteriors for Interpretable and Controllable Discrete Diffusion
authors: Koulischer, Van De Velde, Remy, Develder, Demeester
summary: The authors track the class-conditional posterior online during discrete (masked) diffusion by combining conditional and unconditional model predictions. This posterior gives interpretable dynamics and enables logical guidance (AND, OR, NOT), and they point out that discrete classifier-free guidance mixes data distributions whereas continuous CFG mixes marginals.
takeaways: The class posterior can be updated step by step from conditional vs unconditional predictions, without a separate classifier.
Logical compositions of conditions (including NOT, i.e. avoiding a class) become possible in discrete diffusion.
Discrete and continuous CFG are not the same object: one mixes data distributions, the other mixes marginals.
relevance: Directly relevant to guiding your masked-diffusion / CTMC models of isoform counts — e.g. conditioning on cell type or steering away from a state — and the CFG mismatch point is worth checking before you port continuous guidance tricks.

title: Generative diffusion in long-range correlated landscapes: Speciation cascade and the foam structure of the score
summary: Using an analytically tractable data model (the Gibbs measure of a high-dimensional random potential with long-range correlations), the authors study the exact score of a variance-exploding diffusion. The single speciation threshold becomes a speciation window in which the reverse process commits to ever finer branches of a hierarchy of states, and the score looks like a "foam" of cells separated by shock-like boundaries.
takeaways: For hierarchically structured data, commitment to a mode happens progressively over a window of noise levels, not at one threshold.
The exact score is piecewise smooth with sharp boundaries between cells — a "foam".
Those boundaries may be where trained models misplace probability mass.
relevance: An exploratory spark: a physics view of why the full reverse process matters. The hierarchy picture (coarse class first, finer states later) is a nice lens for cell types → subtypes → isoform usage in your generative models.

title: scAnyOmics: Foundation-Model Distillation for Any-to-Any Completion of Multi-omics Virtual Cells
summary: scAnyOmics distils a frozen single-cell foundation model into a multimodal student that maps scRNA-seq, protein markers and scATAC-seq into one shared representation, so any missing modality can be predicted from the ones observed. It is trained on 690,880 cells from six public studies with paired and partially paired measurements and evaluated on held-out donors.
takeaways: Any-to-any completion: one shared latent is used to reconstruct whichever modality is missing, rather than training a separate model per direction.
Knowledge from a frozen foundation model is transferred by distillation, which lets partially paired data contribute.
Reported to beat baselines on held-out donors, and also used for cell-type annotation, perturbation-response prediction and biological-age estimation.
relevance: This is the same problem shape as scIso — predicting an unmeasured layer (isoforms) from a measured one (gene expression) — so its handling of partially paired data and foundation-model distillation is a useful comparison point for how you train with few long-read cells and many short-read ones.

title: An ODE-based Sampler for Discrete Diffusion Models
authors: Gourevitch, Janati, Moulines, Xing, Durmus, Zanella
summary: The paper asks whether discrete (CTMC) diffusion has an analogue of the probability-flow ODE and answers yes with exponential residual flows: each token carries a continuous residual that evolves by a piecewise ODE driven by the current state and the forward/backward rate matrices, and the discrete state jumps when a residual hits zero. They prove the construction preserves the diffusion's marginals and specialise it to masked and uniform diffusion.
takeaways: All the randomness can be moved into the initial residuals, so after initialisation the sampler is deterministic yet keeps the CTMC marginals exactly.
Jumps happen when a residual reaches zero — essentially an exponential-clock construction of the jump times, made deterministic given the clocks.
Deterministic trajectories make consistency distillation possible for discrete diffusion; they report gains over earlier approaches on code and text generation.
relevance: Your lattice-simplex generator-matching models are CTMCs, so a marginal-preserving deterministic sampler is directly applicable — and could enable few-step distilled sampling of isoform counts. Worth checking whether the construction needs a factorised (per-token) rate, since your jumps move counts between isoforms under a fixed gene total.

title: Second-order Sinkhorn Geometry and √n-Inference
summary: Building on a formal Riemannian metric tensor that quadratically approximates the Sinkhorn divergence, the authors derive its Levi-Civita covariant derivative and obtain geodesic and parallel-transport equations as ODEs in a fixed RKHS. Linearising these gives √n Gaussian limits and bootstrap consistency for plug-in estimates of the exponential and log maps, parallel transport and the induced distance.
takeaways: The Sinkhorn divergence is not a metric, but it can be given a formal Riemannian structure on the space of measures via a quadratic approximation.
With a covariant derivative, geodesics and parallel transport become smooth ODEs on a fixed RKHS — much more tractable than in Wasserstein geometry.
They claim the first √n limit theorems and bootstrap consistency for geometric operations in a transport geometry on measures.
relevance: A spark connecting your OT and differential-geometry tracks: tangent spaces, log maps and parallel transport between cell populations, with uncertainty. A possible tool for comparing distributions of isoform proportions across cell types with error bars.

title: Learning developmental dynamics from lineage context
summary: Introduces 'lineage inpainting', a generative model that uses the states of a cell's relatives in a lineage tree as context, combining tree-structured transformers with stochastic interpolants to model cell-state dynamics. On a lineage-traced mouse embryogenesis atlas it recovers dynamics not visible from expression alone, such as transcriptional convergence of distinct lineages.
takeaways: Lineage context (sisters, cousins) is treated as conditioning information for a stochastic-interpolant generative model over cell states.
It resolves convergence events where different lineages reach a common transcriptional state.
Although trained only on unperturbed development, simulated counterfactuals agree in many cases with observed knockout phenotypes, including a single-cell Tbx5 knockout measurement.
relevance: A worked example of interpolant-based single-cell generation with structured, set-like context — close to your scIso conditioning question and to the Set Transformer / scLDM idea of treating cells as sets.

title: End-to-End Guarantees for Masked Diffusion Models under Conditional Mixing
summary: Gives an end-to-end KL bound for masked diffusion models with a learned denoiser, for sources whose masked-token posteriors depend only weakly on distant tokens ('conditional mixing', correlation length τ_c). Training sample complexity is independent of sequence length, and a dilated schedule needs only O(τ_c log(N|V|/ε)) unmasking steps versus Ω(N) for a fixed random order.
takeaways: Bounds KL(data‖sampler) ≤ ε + N·ε′, combining training error and sampling error rather than assuming an exact denoiser.
The number of training sequences needed scales with τ_c log|V| in the exponent, which the paper shows is minimax-optimal up to constants.
Block-autoregressive samplers chain across blocks with no added error.
relevance: If you use masked diffusion over isoform tokens, this tells you when parallel unmasking is safe: it hinges on how local the dependencies are — worth asking how 'mixing' isoforms within a gene really are.

title: Annealed sampling of diffusion models in lattice field theory
summary: Trains an energy-based diffusion model by score matching, then samples it exactly using stochastic normalizing flows or flow-transformed replica exchange (T-REX), choosing the sampler after training. Tested on scalar field theory and the O(3) sigma model, it follows the predicted exactness and scaling and clearly beats samplers without a learned component.
takeaways: Parameterising the diffusion model as an energy lets you plug it into annealing/MCMC samplers with exactness guarantees.
Training (score matching) and sampling (SNF or T-REX) are decoupled, so the sampler can be swapped later.
Local-footprint energy models keep gradients and divergences cheap on lattices.
relevance: A spark from physics: the EBM-as-diffusion idea connects to the guidance and SMC-style sampling papers on your path, and shows how to make a learned diffusion prior exact at sampling time.

title: H-GLow: Accelerating Graph Generation via Hazard-Guided Discrete Flow Matching
summary: Decomposes a CTMC generator into hazards (how fast something jumps) and conditional jump distributions (where it goes), and uses them to plan graph edits and adapt the sampling time to how active the graph is. It plugs into pretrained graph DFM models and also proposes a new model trained with conditional generator matching to predict hazards and jumps directly.
takeaways: The CTMC generator splits into an exit rate (hazard) and a jump kernel, and these can drive the sampler rather than a fixed time grid.
The proposed objective decomposes exactly into hazard matching plus hazard-weighted jump prediction.
Reported gains: better graph quality with substantially fewer sampling steps on molecular and synthetic benchmarks.
relevance: Very close to your lattice-simplex CTMC models: a hazard/jump parametrisation of the generator could be a natural way to model isoform-count moves under a fixed gene total, and the adaptive-time sampler speaks directly to sampling cost.

title: How Geometry Shapes Generative Model Evaluation on Riemannian Manifolds
summary: Compares geodesic, ambient and tangent-space versions of Wasserstein distance and MMD for evaluating generative models on manifolds of different curvature and dimension, using controlled-noise perturbations and Riemannian Flow Matching samples. Finds that no metric is uniformly reliable and gives reporting and calibration recommendations.
takeaways: On manifolds, curvature and dimension change distances and volume growth, so the choice of evaluation distance changes the measured gap.
Geodesic, ambient and tangent-space metrics can disagree in both magnitude and noise sensitivity.
Recommendation: report the evaluation distance and calibrate metrics to the geometry of the samples.
relevance: Your simplex models live on a curved space (e.g. under the Fisher–Rao view); this is a useful checklist for how you report sample quality for isoform proportions, and it fits yesterday's UDL Ch. 14 on evaluating generative models.

title: HELICS: Biobank-scale Conditional Synthetic Genome Generation via Latent Flow Matching
summary: Generates genome-wide SNP genotypes by compressing each chromosome with a convolutional autoencoder (>600K SNPs to 4,096 latent tokens) and training a transformer conditional flow-matching model on the concatenated latents, trained on 417K UK Biobank genomes. Conditioning on ancestry and genetic-liability summaries steers generation.
takeaways: Latent flow matching makes an ultra-high-dimensional discrete distribution tractable without haplotype phasing.
Reported to preserve allele frequencies and local and long-range SNP correlation better than haplotype-based simulators.
Raising the conditioned disease liability shifts generated SNP dosages in a way that correlates with published association weights.
relevance: A spark from genetics: the same 'discrete data → continuous latent → flow matching' route you could contrast with your direct CTMC-on-counts approach, and conditional synthetic cohorts are an interesting analogue for scIso-style conditional generation.

title: Birth, Death and Diff: Insertion-Based Sequence Generation with Corrections
summary: Insertion-based masked diffusion models generate variable-length sequences by interleaving mask insertion with unmasking, but their decisions are irreversible, so aggressive parallel decoding accumulates errors. δMDM adds substitution and deletion operations, is trained on its own aggressive-decoding mistakes, and interleaves correction steps at inference.
takeaways: Irreversibility is what forces conservative (many-NFE) decoding in masked/insertion diffusion; making states revisable relaxes it.
Training on errors induced by aggressive unmasking teaches the model to correct itself.
Pareto-dominates FlexMDM on speed vs quality; halves generative perplexity on OpenWebText at the highest budget and matches TinyGSM accuracy with half the NFEs.
relevance: A neat example of enriching a CTMC's jump set (insert, substitute, delete) beyond pure unmasking — directly relevant if your lattice-simplex generator ever needs moves that 'undo' earlier count allocations.

title: Active Learning of Conditional Generative Models via the Transport Neural Tangent Kernel
summary: When experiments produce distributions (e.g. single-cell perturbation responses), mean-based active learning ignores distributional shape. The authors decompose Wasserstein test risk into mean and shape terms and propose the transport NTK, which measures how sensitive a model's predicted distribution is to its parameters, and use it as a GP covariance to pick informative conditions.
takeaways: Wasserstein test risk = mean term + shape term, so mean-based acquisition is blind to shape.
tNTK recovers the standard NTK in the deterministic limit and upper-bounds posterior Fréchet variance under small parameter perturbations.
Beats the conditional-mean NTK across conditional flow matching and Monge-gap models, including single-cell perturbation data.
relevance: Combines three of your threads — GPs, conditional flow matching and single-cell perturbation modelling — and the 'which condition to measure next' question maps onto choosing cell types or tissues for isoform-resolved sequencing.

title: Escaping cells dilute CRISPR screen responses unequally across cell types
summary: In single-cell CRISPR screens, cells that escaped knockdown keep growing while knocked-down cells are depleted, so the measured response is diluted. A two-group mixture on the targeted gene's counts estimates this escape fraction, which reaches about half of cells in hESCs and shrinks responses to (1−e)² of the true effect.
takeaways: The escape fraction rises with gene essentiality and differs between cell types.
Dilution biases cross-cell-type transfer models and rewards benchmark predictions shrunk towards no change.
Response sizes should be compared on knocked-down cells or corrected for escape.
relevance: A spark from the data side: if you ever train or benchmark perturbation models (e.g. for isoform responses), this is a simple count-mixture correction that changes what the 'ground truth' even is.

title: Trajectory Matching: Discrete Flow Matching with Structured Actions
summary: Most discrete flow matching conditions only on endpoints and so is limited to independent, component-wise edits on fixed-size states. Trajectory matching instead conditions on a full sequence of user-defined actions connecting the endpoints (attach a fragment, add a node with its edge, grow a child), giving simulation-free training targets. They prove the objective recovers the marginal flow and strictly subsumes factorised DFM; on MOSES molecule generation validity rises from 92.8% to 99.2%.
takeaways: Conditioning on a whole action path rather than just endpoints makes non-factorising and size-changing actions tractable.
The marginal flow is still recovered, so this is a generalisation of DFM, not an approximation.
The action vocabulary becomes a modelling choice — domain-aligned actions help structured outputs.
relevance: Your lattice-simplex CTMC moves single counts between isoforms under a fixed gene total; this framework lets you define richer, structured moves (e.g. shifting mass between isoforms that share exons) while keeping a principled generator-matching target.

title: Generative Modeling via Nonlinear Schrödinger Bridges and Branching Diffusions
summary: The authors extend the Schrödinger bridge to a nonlinear version (SBNL) defined by coupled forward–backward PDEs from mean-field game theory, so the bridge can include interaction terms and convex penalties. They solve it with branching diffusions — a probabilistic representation of semilinear PDEs — which is embarrassingly parallel and scales to high dimension. The method recovers the classical bridge, handles Gross–Pitaevskii-type and potential interactions, and generates MNIST and FFHQ images; score-based diffusion and Gaussian Schrödinger bridges appear as special cases.
takeaways: Classical Schrödinger bridges are the linear case of a mean-field-game PDE system; adding nonlinearity lets samples interact.
Branching diffusions give a simulation-based, parallel solver for the resulting semilinear PDEs.
Diffusion models and tractable Gaussian bridges sit inside the framework as special cases.
relevance: Bridges between populations are a natural tool for perturbation modelling (control vs perturbed cells); the interaction term is a way to encode population-level constraints, such as matching a target marginal, which links to the Jeffrey guidance paper you read yesterday.

title: Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations
summary: Contrastive multimodal models like CLIP leave a persistent gap between image and text embeddings on the sphere. Moving the embeddings onto the probability simplex with lightweight softmax adapters and a Total Variation similarity reduces the centroid gap by 97–99% across five retrieval benchmarks while matching or beating retrieval of unconstrained models.
takeaways: Sphere and simplex share intrinsic dimension, but the simplex's non-negativity and unit-mass constraints act as a shared coordinate system.
TV distance replaces cosine similarity as the natural similarity on the simplex.
A purely geometric change, with small adapters, nearly closes the modality gap.
relevance: A spark: the simplex as a representation space rather than a data space. Your isoform proportions already live there — it's a nudge to think about which similarity (TV, Fisher–Rao, Aitchison) your models implicitly use on it.

title: Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks
authors: Casado Noguerales, von Rütte, Schölkopf, Hofmann & Raoufi
summary: Masked and uniform discrete diffusion destroy a token's identity in one jump, so noisy states can't express 'one of these few options'. Binary Discrete Diffusion is a continuous-time process whose state is a set of candidate tokens per position (a binary membership vector), changed by adding and removing candidates. It beats tuned masked and uniform baselines on Sudoku-Extreme, Boxoban and graph colouring, and stays competitive on language modelling.
takeaways: The choice of corruption kernel changes what the reverse model learns, not just its efficiency.
Candidate sets let information be lost and recovered gradually, representing partial uncertainty in the state itself.
Gains are largest on the hardest constraint-satisfaction instances.
relevance: A worked example of designing the forward CTMC kernel rather than defaulting to masking — directly relevant to your choice of noising process on the lattice simplex, where intermediate states could likewise encode partially resolved isoform assignments.

title: Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models
summary: Reward guidance samples an exponential tilt of the base density, usually via an extra drift term or reweighted transitions ('external guidance'). For discrete data on {−1,1}^d the authors show the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted, rescaled input, so guidance can change where the denoiser is evaluated instead. Training with random diagonal rescalings lets a single network handle these out-of-distribution inputs, sampling reward tilts, class labels and infilling without fine-tuning.
takeaways: Tilting can be implemented by moving the denoiser's input rather than adding a guidance term.
The exact result holds for linear tilts of discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube.
Training-time data augmentation (random rescalings) is what makes the shifted evaluations reliable.
relevance: Pairs naturally with today's Jeffrey guidance paper (also a tilt p(x)ρ(u(x))): together they give two routes — external vs internal — to steer a pretrained discrete generator like yours towards a target.

title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
summary: On the flat 1D torus, the authors construct a case where a recent likelihood-based extension of Riemannian flow matching is optimised by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data. They define 'compatibility' — the objective's population minimiser recovers the true marginal velocity — give a general condition for it, and propose an exponential-family objective over endpoints that is compatible and only puts mass on feasible velocities. It improves NLL on two of four sphere geospatial benchmarks and on high-dimensional tori.
takeaways: A flow matching loss can be globally optimal yet point the wrong way if it isn't compatible.
On compact manifolds, some objectives put density on infeasible velocities.
The fix amounts to a reweighting of the FM loss that treats speed and direction errors differently on constant-curvature manifolds.
relevance: A spark from geometry: the simplex in your work also has boundaries and feasibility constraints, and the 'is my loss's minimiser actually the marginal field?' check is a useful sanity test for any non-Euclidean flow matching variant you design.
Same design question as your source-conditioned models: what to put at t = 0. A gene-level prediction (as in scIso) could serve as the source, with the flow learning only the isoform-level residual.
summary: For combinatorial perturbations, most of the response is the sum of single-perturbation effects. SynGeneFlow anchors the flow's source distribution at that additive prior and learns only the residual flow to the true perturbed state.
takeaways: Choosing an informative source distribution focuses model capacity on the hard, non-additive part of the signal.
Gene-gene interactions enter as a static mask plus a perturbation-dependent bias in the network.
MMD regularisation on both the endpoint and the residual distributions keeps population-level structure.
title: Synergy-Aware Residual Flow Matching for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction (SynGeneFlow)

relevance: The current argument for continuous flows over discrete diffusion on discrete data. Useful context for your choice between a CTMC on the lattice simplex and continuous simplex flows, and it connects to the flow-map papers already on your path.
summary: A continuous flow language model scaled to 8B parameters by adapting a pretrained autoregressive model: causal attention over the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. Trained on fewer than 30B tokens.
takeaways: Matches or beats the autoregressive base on instruction following, reasoning and coding, and can be distilled into flow maps for one- or few-step generation.
Flow training acts like multi-token prediction and can even improve the AR capabilities it starts from.
A self-speculative decoding scheme (flow drafts, AR verification in one model) gives about 2.5x AR throughput and beats discrete diffusion at comparable quality.
title: Large Flow Language Models (Lafa)

relevance: A cheap upgrade to try in your hierarchical NB + multinomial VAE baseline: swap the standard normal prior for this one and compare ELBOs and cell-type clustering. David Knowles also works on splicing (LeafCutter), so his group may follow up on isoform-level models.
summary: Revisits the VampPrior, which approximates the optimal VAE prior (the aggregate posterior) with a mixture of encoder outputs at learned pseudo-inputs. It fixes two weaknesses: prior and posterior share one amortised covariance, and the mixture weights are fixed and uniform.
takeaways: Decoupling the prior and posterior covariances removes a conflict between wanting high-entropy priors and low-entropy posteriors, and raises model evidence.
Replacing the uniform mixture with a Dirichlet process gives non-parametric clustering in latent space.
Dropping the new prior into scVI improves integration and clustering across six single-cell atlases. Only the prior changes, so it works with any continuous-latent DLVM.
title: VampPrior Unleashed
